VIII. ROSHANAK LISTENS

The recording ends. There is a moment of silence on the tape — eleven seconds, though she does not know this yet, will not notice until she plays it back months later, will sit with it when she does — and then the sound of a chair moving, and Darya switching off the mixer, and Nazanin coming in from the kitchen with the tea that nobody asked for.
This is the last entry of the last notebook of Manuchehr Delgoshā. He did not know it was the last entry. He was thinking about the tea.
Six months later.
Roshanak listens in a small room at the back of the Dāstān-khāne office. Darya has given her the room, the headphones, and four hours. She has been listening for two.
It is the first time she has heard the recording.

She did not listen when they made it. She was there — she was in the room, she asked the questions, she sat across from him in the kitchen chair while he sat in his chair, the one four degrees off — but being in the room is not the same as listening. In the room you are managing the room. You are watching the face, tracking the pause, deciding whether to ask the next question or let the silence do it. You are not listening. You are working.
Now she is listening.
The recording took place on a Friday.

This was Roshanak’s choice. She had said Friday because the archive does not record on Fridays by default — a scheduling buffer they had inherited from some earlier administrative decision nobody remembered making — and she wanted his session to have no default. She wanted it to sit outside the ordinary week.
I did not argue.
I had been arguing less lately. Not because I had run out of things to argue about. Because arguing requires a certain confidence that you will be here to hear the response.

The machine Roshanak brought was smaller than I expected. A grey box, roughly the size of the medical bag Nazanin carries, with a single indicator light that turned green when it was ready and did nothing else. No waveforms. No display. No numbers. Just the green light, and then you speak, and somewhere inside the grey box the speaking becomes a file.

I sat in the chair. Not the writing chair — I had not been clear about which chair I wanted and Roshanak had assumed the kitchen chair, the one near the window that gets the light in the afternoon. It was not the right chair. But sitting in the right chair and speaking into a machine felt like the kind of theater I did not need at this point in my life. So I sat in the kitchen chair and I looked at the green light and I said nothing for approximately two minutes.

Roshanak did not prompt me. She had learned this from somewhere, probably from the dozens of sessions she had already run for the archive, the way a long silence is not a failure but a gathering. She sat to my left and slightly behind me, where I could not easily see her, which was also her choice, and I appreciated it enough to say nothing about it.

Nazanin had made tea. She had left the tea on the counter and gone into the other room because she had decided, without being asked, that her presence in the doorway would make me perform instead of speak. She told me this afterward. This was a perceptive reading of my psychology for someone who had only known me for fourteen months. Fourteen months is plenty of time. Then she poured herself a second cup and told me to stop fishing for compliments.
Here is what I did not tell Roshanak, before I started speaking:
I had written my name on a piece of paper that morning.

Not Delgoshā. Not the three names. My name. The name my mother says when she forgets I am there. The name Payam used when we were twenty and nothing had happened yet. The name I gave away to a notebook and never took back.
I wrote it and I looked at it for a while and then I folded the paper and put it in my jacket pocket.
I spoke into the machine under my own name, for the first time in a public document, in forty-eight years.
I don’t know if that is funny. Probably it is funny. Most things, at sufficient distance, are funny.
Roshanak pressed the record button. The green light stayed green.
I said: Fine. But I want it known that I disagreed with this.

She laughed — a surprised laugh, involuntary, the kind she would have suppressed if she had been faster. The machine caught it. It is in the file. When you listen to the recording you can hear, in the first four seconds, the sound of her deciding to let it stay.
She let it stay.
I decided to earn that.
She heard the graduation speech before she gave it.

Not in a room. He sent it through Vahid with a note — the only note she ever received in his own words, in forty-seven years, the only time he broke the protocol of the arrangement. The note said: This is the one I would give. If you change anything, make it shorter.

She read it in her flat at two in the morning. She read it three times. The third time she laughed — not the audience laugh, not the performer’s laugh, but the private one, the one she did not use at work, the one that meant: this is true.

She performed it in front of nine hundred people at Sharif. Ranked third, behind the rector and the setar. She called Manu — the first time she called him directly, the first time she had his number — and said: third. He’d heard. Behind the setar. The setar was good? Very good. He was quiet for a moment. That’s acceptable.
I want to meet you. You don’t. I do. You want to meet the person who wrote it. That person doesn’t meet people. Manu. Yes. I’m going to call you again. I know.
She called him every Wednesday after that.
For eleven years.

She called him to complain. To read him things she was working on and hear him say shorter. To tell him what the room was doing, which he could not see and needed to know. To argue about a word — always a single word, somewhere in the third or fourth beat of a piece, a word she thought was wrong and he was certain was right, and they would argue about it for forty minutes and she would perform it his way and he would be right, which she never said, which he never required her to say, which was its own kind of calibration.

She called him the night her father died and said nothing about her father. She talked about a joke she was developing. He let her. At the end: is there something else. No. Fine. And then, before she could hang up: I’m sorry. You don’t know what for. I know enough.
She has not told anyone about this.
On the headphones, his voice says: Two specific laughs. In the back third of the room. Those two laughs are the thing I am most proud of in forty-seven years.
She stops the recording.
She sits in the small room at the back of the Dāstān-khāne office.

She thinks about Karaj. The room in Karaj, forty people — no, more, it was a bigger room by then, three hundred people — and the line he wrote, the line about the family, the one about the fixed address, and the laugh that came back from the back third of the room, two people, out of sync with the rest of the audience, the real laugh, the unmanaged one, the one that means: yes, that is exactly the weight, I knew the weight and was pretending otherwise and now someone has said it.
She did not know he was counting. She did not know he was tracking the individual laughs, the specific two, the ones in the back third.
She thought she was delivering his material.
He was watching from the outside.
From forty hours in the future, refracted through fifty-eight years of notebooks, he was watching.
She presses play.
His voice again. The water break. The sound of him setting the glass down. And then:
Roshanak. I want to say something and I want you to leave it in the recording.

She remembers this moment. She remembers sitting across from him in the kitchen chair and watching his face say the thing he had been not-saying for eleven years. She was not going to cry then. She was working. She was managing the room.
She is not managing anything now.
And then she hears it.
Nazanin has been coming every day for eight months.

His voice, in the recording, saying it the same way he said everything — flat, accurate, certain. She arrives at eight-thirty. She leaves at six. In between she does not say very much, and what she says is accurate to a degree I find unsettling.
He trusted her.

Of course he trusted her. He trusted her from the second week, from the moment she said you’ll want it in eleven minutes and was correct. He had told Roshanak about her on a Wednesday in Mehr — I have a caretaker now, she comes every day, I don’t know who arranged it — and Roshanak had said, very carefully: that’s good, you needed someone. He said: yes. She did not ask how the arrangement had been made. He did not pursue it. He had assumed the ophthalmologist. Or Payam. Or the invisible machinery of people who love a person and do practical things about it without saying so.
He never asked.
The arrangement was hers.

She had known about the recording for two years before it happened. Not the archive — the archive came later, after Darya, after the grandmother in Tabriz, after Roshanak understood what she was building and understood that Manu’s voice needed to be in it while there was still a Manu. She had known, for two years, that she needed him prepared. Not coached. Not directed. Prepared the way a room is prepared — the equipment set out, the acoustics checked, the quality of the light adjusted without comment so that when the moment came it felt natural and inevitable and like no one had done anything at all.

Nazanin was a third-year archivist at the Dāstān-khāne. She had run eleven sessions by the time Roshanak asked her. She was, of all the people Roshanak had trained, the one whose quality of presence was most precisely what Manu would need: she did not insert herself into other people’s processing. She said accurate things at the wrong moment, which is a quality that cannot be taught, and which is the quality his material ran on. Roshanak had watched her in sessions and thought: he will trust this person. He will not know why. He will trust her in the second week, before he has made a decision about it, and by the third month he will have reorganised his entire morning around her presence, and he will not notice that he has done this.
She was correct about all of it.
She asked Nazanin in Ābān 1426.

She told her almost everything. Not the archive — she did not want Nazanin to perform preparation, she wanted her to do the work the work required, and the archive was not the work’s purpose, the work’s purpose was Manu’s last year at full capacity. She told her about the notebooks. About the third hour. About Pesar Khaleh and the syrup and the chair and the way he processed things in silence if you let him. She told her about Payam in the cell. About the eleven words. She said: he is going to die in the next few years and he knows it and nobody is saying it and he needs someone in the room who can hear what he is not saying.
Nazanin said: what do I tell him about how I was hired.
Roshanak said: tell him the ophthalmologist. If he asks. He won’t ask.
He didn’t ask.
She knew, when she arranged it, that he would not want to know.

This is the part she has not been able to make peace with. Not the arrangement — the arrangement was the right thing, the months with Nazanin were the best months, she heard it in his voice on the Wednesday calls, a steadiness that had not been there before, a willingness to say things aloud that he had previously only written. The arrangement gave him the last year he had. She does not regret the arrangement.
She regrets the not-telling.

She should have told him. At some point — after the recording, after the archive session, after the Mehr festival, sometime in the last four months when it was clear that the time was contracting and the things that had not been said needed to be said — she should have told him. I arranged this. Nazanin is mine. She was placed. You were prepared.
She did not.

She could not decide whether the telling would have been for him or for her. Whether the thing she needed to confess was the thing he needed to know. Whether a man who spent forty-seven years being invisible in his own work, who had built the architecture of invisibility and inhabited it completely and on purpose, would find it a violation or a confirmation — of course. Of course someone arranged the conditions. This is how the good material comes. Someone sets it out and says nothing.
She didn’t tell him.
He died not knowing.

And now his voice is in her ears saying Nazanin has been coming every day for eight months with the complete trust of a person who believes the arrangement was accidental, who believes the eight months were simply what happened, who never turned the question sideways to look at the weight of it.
She sits in the small room.
She does not stop the recording.
Six months later, Roshanak sits in the archive room and presses play.

She has been putting this off. Not because she did not want to hear it — she has thought about the recording almost every day since he died — but because listening requires a kind of preparation she has been unable to make. You cannot prepare for someone’s voice. You can only decide to hear it, and then you hear it, and you discover that preparation would not have helped anyway.
His voice arrives in the room like he arrived in rooms.

No announcement. No adjustment period. Suddenly he is simply there, speaking, in the middle of a sentence he seems to have started before anyone was ready for it. Fine. But I want it known that I disagreed with this. Her own laugh in the background — that involuntary laugh she remembers making — and then his voice, settling, dropping half a register, the way it always did when he was about to say something he had been thinking about for a long time.
She sits very still.

Outside, the city is doing what cities do in October: contracting slightly, pulling its collar up, preparing for the long interior season. She can hear traffic through the window. She does not close the window. She wants the city in the room while she listens. She wants something ordinary happening at the same time.
She does not cry during the funny parts, which is when she expected to cry.

She cries during the part where he describes his father reading the material in the scrapyard. His father’s hands on the pages — the pages being turned sideways so they would not blow away — his father holding a page up to the light because the print was small. She had not known this image. He had never given it to her directly. And here it is, surfacing in the machine’s recording like something that had been waiting under water, patient, unhurried, the way grief is patient and unhurried when it knows it has already won.
She is crying before she knows she is crying.

This is the specific grief of losing a person you have not yet finished learning. Not the grief of what was taken — the jokes, the arguments, the sarcasm delivered with the precision of a scalpel — but the grief of what kept arriving even after the arrival was supposed to stop. Every sentence in the recording is evidence of a depth she will now never finish measuring. He is still going further. He is going further right now, in this room, in October, with the city outside making its ordinary sounds, and he is not here to stop himself, and she cannot ask him to slow down, and there are forty-seven more minutes of this.
She does not stop the recording.
At the part where he talks about Pesar Khaleh, she laughs and then covers her mouth, as though the laugh might disturb someone.
There is no one to disturb. He is dead. The laugh is fine.

She takes her hand away from her mouth. She lets herself laugh at the part where he says I did not name the algorithm after Payam to honor Payam. I named it after Payam to annoy Payam. These are different things. Payam knows the difference. Payam has not said anything about it because Payam is, grudgingly, amused. This took eight years.

She laughs and cries at the same time, which is the condition he spent forty-seven years trying to produce in other people, in rooms full of strangers, with nothing but language and timing. He managed it, finally, here, in an empty archive room, six months after he died, with an audience of one.
She thinks: he would find this acceptable.
She thinks: he would say acceptable is not the word, but it will do.
She listens to all of it.
When it ends, the machine returns to its standby tone — a small, neutral sound, indifferent to what it has just held — and she sits for a while in the afterward.

There is a Persian expression — del-tangī [del-tan-GEE], literally chest-tightness — used for the specific ache of missing someone. Not the sharp grief of new loss but the older, settled kind: the ache that has learned to live in the body without asking permission. She has known the word her whole life. She has never felt it this precisely before.

She closes the archive file. She labels it correctly. She backs it up in three places, which is the archive’s protocol, and which she now understands was always about this: the terror of a voice becoming unreachable.
Then she turns off the light and goes home.
She stops the recording when it ends.
Eleven seconds of silence. Then the sound of a chair. Then Darya switching off the mixer. Then Nazanin with the tea.
She takes off the headphones.
She sits for a while.

Then she picks up her phone and opens the Dāstān-khāne scheduling app and books the interview for tomorrow — a woman in Tabriz, eighty-three years old, who says she has something to tell her about cheese.
She does not know what it is. She does not know if it will be funny or sad or somewhere in between, which is where most true things live.

She knows she will ask the questions and the woman will talk and the archive will keep it and nobody will file the serial numbers off and nobody will make it shorter and the weight will be exactly what it is.
Everywhere in the world.

And that was all.
And that was all.
And that was all.
How many entries in this notebook?
One hundred and three.
In total — this one and the others?
[the machine counts]
Hm.
Is that right?
Yes.
Hm.
[Nazanin, from the kitchen: do you want tea?]
Yes.

He opened the door and the light came in and he said nothing because there was nothing left to say that the light had not already said and the room heard it and the room understood and the scribe closed the book.
A NOTE FROM THE SERIES EDITOR
from the Delgoshā, Nos. 68–103
Manuchehr Delgoshā — which is not his name, but it is the name he gave us, and we will use it — requested, in the voice recording that closes this book, that he be cremated.
He gave three reasons.
The first: I do not want to be findable.
The second: The concept of a fixed location for my remains implies a schedule, and I have never kept a schedule.
The third: Honestly, I think it would be funny.
We cremated him.

His ashes are in the custody of Roshanak Sadeghi [row-sha-NAAK saa-de-GHEE], series editor from No. 91 forward, interviewer for the Dāstān-khāne archive, the person who pressed record on a Friday and laughed at the first thing he said and did not edit it out.

She did not ask for custody. She was asked, by a notarized letter that arrived four months before the recording and sat in the archive’s incoming mail for three weeks because she thought it was about the archive’s licensing agreement and did not open it promptly. When she opened it she called Darya and read it aloud on the phone. Darya said: of course it was you. Roshanak said: I haven’t even agreed yet. Darya said: Roshanak. She agreed.
He was sixty-eight. He would have said this was not young. He would have been wrong.
He was right about the ashes.
They do carry the same dry humor. We cannot explain this. The container is a brushed-tin cylinder that he specified himself, with a label he also specified, which reads:
REFRIGERATE.
Below this, in smaller print:
No. 103 of an ongoing conversation.
He appears to have prepared this in advance.

She does not know what she will do with them. This is fine. He did not tell her. He told her, in the letter, that the decision about what to do with a person is a decision that belongs to the living, and I am not going to make it for you from beyond the grave, because I am not a character in a melodrama. He then added a footnote that said: Although. If I were. The scrapyard. Obviously.
She is keeping the option open.

Nazanin is the archive’s archivist for the western district of Tehran. She has been with the Dāstān-khāne since 1425. She conducted the session with the woman in Tabriz who had something to tell her about cheese. She has conducted forty-three sessions since Manu died.

She does not talk about the eight months. She does not talk about Manu. If you ask her about either thing she will look at you for a moment with an expression that gives nothing and then say something accurate at the wrong moment, and you will find yourself laughing, and by the time you recover you will have forgotten what you asked.
He would have found this, if he had known: acceptable. Not the word, but it will do.
He did not know.
He should have known.
I did not tell him. I am writing it here because I could not find another place for it.
— R.S.

The archive continues. The Dāstān-khāne has, at the time this volume goes to press, recorded one hundred and fourteen unwritten stories in their owners’ own voices. Roshanak conducts most of the sessions herself. Darya edits. The archive’s first public release, a collection of forty stories from four cities, is expected in 1429 [2050].
Manu is in the archive. Entry number six, recorded on a Friday in early 1427, twenty-two minutes and forty-seven seconds. Filed under the name he finally used.
Available on request.

The from the Delgoshā interstitials run through this series from No. 68 to No. 103. They begin as a complete line of text and erode, slowly, across nine books, until they are nothing but dots. In this book they reverse: the dots at the front matter open toward the title, and the final interstitial, on the last page, reads without erosion: from the Delgoshā
Complete. For the first time.

We did not plan this. That is, we planned it — Manu and Roshanak planned it, somewhere between Entry 72 and Entry 91, in a conversation that is not recorded anywhere — but it arrived looking like something that had always been going to happen. This is how good endings work. They feel inevitable. They feel like you were reading toward them all along without knowing.
You were.
He knew.
He didn’t say.
The Delgoshā series concludes here.
Thank you for reading.
— R.S.
Tehran / 1428 from the Delgoshā
He asked the wise man: what is the difference between a joke and a prayer?
The wise man said: a joke is a prayer that knows it will not be answered.
He said: and if it is answered?
The wise man said: then it was a prayer.
He said: and if it makes you laugh?
The wise man said: then it was both, and you were the door it passed through.
He said: and the door?
The wise man said nothing.
He stood there for eleven minutes.
Then he wrote it down.

GLOSSARY
Ābān [aa-BAAN] — Persian. The eighth month of the Iranian calendar, in mid-autumn.
Anfarādi [an-fa-RAA-dee] — Persian, individual, solitary. Solitary confinement.
Charles Bonnet [SHAARL bo-NEH] — Charles Bonnet
(1720–1793), Genevan naturalist, who described the silent visual hallucinations of his grandfather; the syndrome of such hallucinations in people with failing sight carries his name.
Darya [DAR-yaa] — Persian, sea. A given name.
Dast-forush [dast-fo-ROOSH] — Persian, hand-seller. A hawker who sells from his hands, on the street or on a moving train.
Dāstān-khāne [daas-TAAN-khaa-NEH] — Persian, story-house. The name of the archive of spoken stories in this book.
Del-tangī [del-tan-GEE] — Persian, tightness of the heart. Missing someone, felt as a pressure in the chest.
Kur [KOOR] — Persian, blind. The blunt word, and generally the one used when the person is not in the room.
Mehr [MEHR] — Persian. The seventh month of the Iranian calendar, at the start of autumn.
Nābinā [naa-bee-NAA] — Persian, without sight. The courteous word, and the one that appears on forms.
Narmak [NAR-mak] — A district in the north-east of Tehran.
Payam [pa-YAAM] — Persian, message. A given name.
Pesar khāleh [pe-SAR khaa-LEH] — Persian, maternal aunt’s son.
A cousin; and, capitalised, the name of the writing machine in this book.
Romanu [roh-MAA-noo] — The name filed on the archive’s first recording.
Roshanak [ro-sha-NAK] — Persian, little light. A given name.
Sekkeh [SEK-keh] — Persian, coin. In ordinary speech, a gold coin held as savings.
Setār [se-TAAR] — Persian, three strings. A long-necked Persian lute, played with the nail of the index finger.
Shahrivar [sha-ree-VAR] — Persian. The sixth month of the Iranian calendar, at the end of summer.
Ta’ārof [ta-AA-rof] — Arabic via Persian, mutual acquaintance. The system of ritual courtesy in which an offer is refused two or three times before it is accepted.
Zabt [ZABT] — Arabic via Persian, recording, seizure. A recording; also the official seizure of a thing.
